Day 2 Convective Outlook  
NWS Storm Prediction Center Norman OK
1231 PM CDT Fri Aug 07 2026

Valid 081200Z - 091200Z

...THERE IS A MARGINAL RISK OF SEVERE THUNDERSTORMS WITHIN PARTS OF
THE CENTRAL AND NORTHERN PLAINS INTO THE MID/UPPER MISSISSIPPI
VALLEY...PARTS OF CENTRAL/SOUTHEAST ARIZONA...PARTS OF THE
MID-ATLANTIC...

...SUMMARY...
Thunderstorms with severe wind gusts will be possible Saturday
afternoon and evening across parts of the central and northern
Plains southeastward into the lower to mid Missouri Valley.
Additional strong to severe storms are possible in the Mid-Atlantic
and central/southeast Arizona.

...Central Plains into Upper Mississippi Valley...
A complex forecast scenario continues to be evident on Saturday.
Models continue to show a focused low-level jet into western
Nebraska/South Dakota early Saturday morning. Some convection may be
associated with this feature, though storm coverage is not clear.
Depending on the evolution of that activity, some risk for severe
winds and large hail is possible. Storm coverage will largely
dictate how long early morning activity can persist into the
afternoon as warming temperatures aloft are expected during the day.
A strong enough cold pool would have to evolve in order to allow
convection to propagate southeastward with the low-level jet
decreasing into the late morning/early afternoon. Convective
development during the afternoon is far from certain given the
aforementioned capping that will exist. Forcing for ascent will be
weak as well. Some guidance does show some thunderstorm development
along the cold front in parts of the eastern Dakotas/western
Minnesota. The Marginal has been expanded into these areas to
account for this potential hail/wind threat.

By late afternoon/early evening, an intensifying low-level jet will
be focused within the Mid-Missouri Valley. Storm development will
become more likely along the warm front as this occurs. However, the
strongest activity may not form until around 06Z. This reduces
confidence in how severe the activity will be, particularly in terms
of severe wind. Again, the Marginal was expanded to the north/east
to encompass the various model solutions. Large hail would be
possible even with elevated storms given sufficient shear and steep
mid-level lapse rates. A greater threat for severe wind gusts may
still develop, but this is conditional on enough of a cold pool
developing. Confidence remains rather low.

...Mid-Atlantic...
A modest, low-amplitude shortwave trough will be favorably timed
with afternoon heating. Widely scattered to scattered storms are
possible ahead of this feature. Deep-layer shear will not be overly
strong, but should be sufficient for strong/marginally severe cells
and clusters. Storm coverage is not certain given the veered,
deep-layer flow, but most model guidance suggests locally greater
storm coverage from northern Virginia into eastern Pennsylvania and
adjacent New Jersey. Wind damage will be the main concern.

...Arizona...
Low 60s F dewpoints are forecast to remain within the lower desert
areas. Strong heating should promote destabilization during the
afternoon/early evening. Most CAM guidance suggests that one or more
clusters will develop on the Mogollon Rim and move west/southwest.
Severe wind gusts will be possible with this activity.

..Wendt.. 08/07/2026

Day 3 Convective Outlook  
NWS Storm Prediction Center Norman OK
0223 AM CDT Fri Aug 07 2026

Valid 091200Z - 101200Z

...THERE IS A MARGINAL RISK OF SEVERE THUNDERSTORMS FROM PARTS OF
THE CENTRAL AND NORTHERN PLAINS EAST-SOUTHEASTWARD INTO THE SOUTHERN
GREAT LAKES REGION...

...SUMMARY...
Thunderstorms with isolated severe wind gusts and hail will be
possible Sunday afternoon and evening from parts of the central and
northern Plains east-southeastward into the southern Great Lakes
region.

...Central and Northern Plains/Mid Missouri Valley/Southern Great
Lakes...
At the surface, a cold front will advance southward into the
north-central states on Sunday, being positioned from South Dakota
eastward into Wisconsin by afternoon. Surface dewpoints near and to
the south of the front will be in the 60s and 70s F, which will
contribute to the development of moderate instability. Large-scale
ascent over this unstable airmass will remain relatively weak. In
spite of this, isolated thunderstorms are expected to form in areas
where low-level convergence becomes maximized. Model forecasts
suggest that the most favorable locations could be near the front in
South Dakota and from northeastern Nebraska into southern Iowa along
the northern edge of the stronger low-level flow. In both of these
locations, moderate to strong instability coupled with moderate
deep-layer shear should be sufficient for a severe threat. Severe
wind gusts will be the most likely hazard during the late afternoon
and early evening with cell clusters or short line segments that
move southeastward along and near the instability axis. Hail could
also occur mainly in the central and northern Plains, where
mid-level lapse rates will be steepest.

..Broyles.. 08/07/2026

Day 4-8 Convective Outlook  
NWS Storm Prediction Center Norman OK
0359 AM CDT Fri Aug 07 2026

Valid 101200Z - 151200Z

...DISCUSSION...
...Monday/Day 4 to Wednesday/Day 6...
A broad cyclonic flow pattern is forecast to remain in place from
the north-central U.S. to the Northeast during the early to
mid-week. On the southern edge of the stronger flow, it appears that
an east-to-west corridor of moisture and instability will remain in
place from the central Plains eastward into the Midwest. On Monday,
isolated to scattered thunderstorm development will be possible
during the afternoon and evening along and near the northern edge of
the stronger instability, from eastern Nebraska eastward into the
southern Great Lakes. The greatest convective coverage is expected
to be from northern Illinois eastward into western Pennsylvania,
where low-level flow is forecast to be maximized. Moderate
deep-layer shear along this zone is forecast to be favorable for a
severe threat Monday afternoon and evening. Supercells and multicell
line segments will have potential to produce severe wind gusts.

On Tuesday and Wednesday, model forecasts suggest that a front will
move southward into northern sections of the Ohio Valley, while the
instability axis remains in a similar position further west near the
Omaha area. Isolated to scattered thunderstorms will again be
possible in the afternoon and evening, near and to the north of the
instability axis. An isolated severe threat could develop with
storms that form within or near the strongest instability. However,
predictability is low concerning where the greatest potential for
severe storms will be.

...Thursday/Day 7 and Friday/Day 8...
On Thursday and Friday, west to northwesterly mid-level flow is
forecast over much of the eastern half of the nation. A moist and
unstable airmass should be in place from the central and northern
Plains southeastward into the Ohio and Tennessee Valleys. Although
large-scale ascent may be relatively weak over much of this area,
isolated to scattered thunderstorms will be possible across parts of
this airmass during the afternoon and evening. Due to the extended
time range, predictability remains low concerning the finer-scale
details of any scenario from Thursday into Friday.

..Broyles.. 08/07/2026

Day 1 Convective Outlook  
NWS Storm Prediction Center Norman OK
1106 AM CDT Fri Aug 07 2026

Valid 071630Z - 081200Z

...THERE IS A SLIGHT RISK OF SEVERE THUNDERSTORMS ACROSS PARTS OF
SOUTHERN MINNESOTA INTO IOWA...NORTHERN WISCONSIN INTO THE UPPER
PENINSULA OF MICHIGAN...AND THE MID-ATLANTIC...

...SUMMARY...
Isolated to scattered severe thunderstorms are possible across parts
of the Upper Midwest/Great Lakes this afternoon and evening, with
large to very large hail and severe winds the main threats.
Thunderstorms capable of scattered damaging winds may also occur
over portions of the Mid-Atlantic.

...Upper Midwest/Great Lakes...
Thunderstorms are ongoing along/ahead of a cold front late this
morning from the MN Arrowhead southwestward into southern
MN/northern IA. While there are still uncertainties regarding
convective evolution this afternoon and evening, it appears
increasingly probable that two mesoscale corridors of greater severe
potential will exist: one across southern MN into IA, and another
across northern WI into the U.P of MI. In general, the severe risk
today will be aided by a mid/upper-level trough advancing
east-southeastward across these regions in tandem with a 35-50 kt
west-northwesterly mid-level jet.

Thunderstorms are expected to further increase in coverage and
intensity along the eastward-advancing cold front this afternoon
across parts of northern WI into the western U.P of MI. While latest
NAM/RAP forecast soundings across this area suggest low-level
moisture remains fairly shallow/limited, mostly clear conditions are
noted on recent visible satellite imagery. Resultant moderate
instability and gradually strengthening deep-layer shear with the
approach of the mid/upper-level trough will aid in thunderstorm
organization. Small clusters/bowing line segments will probably be
the dominant mode given the linear forcing of the cold front, with
enhanced low/mid-level flow aiding the risk for scattered
severe/damaging winds. A Slight Risk has been added for parts of
northern WI into the U.P of MI given increased confidence in this
scenario occurring.

Farther south, generally elevated convection is ongoing across
southern MN into northern IA. The 12Z observed sounding from MPX
showed fairly steep low/mid-level lapse rates in the 850-530 mb
layer, which along with 35-40 kt of effective bulk shear and around
2000 J/kg of MUCAPE may continue to support a threat for severe hail
with this activity in the short term. Even though cloud cover
remains prevalent across these areas late this morning, a corridor
of moderate to locally strong instability is still forecast to
develop this afternoon across parts of eastern NE into IA ahead of
the cold front. Current expectations are for multiple surface-based
supercells and/or bowing clusters to develop along/ahead of the
front in southern MN, and then spread southeastward across IA
through the late afternoon/early evening. A threat for both large
hail and damaging winds should exist with this activity, and a
Slight Risk has been introduced where confidence is greater that
robust convection will occur. 2+ inch diameter hail and perhaps a
tornado also appear possible with any surface-based supercell, even
though low-level flow will not be overly strong.

...Ohio Valley into the Mid-Atlantic...
Between upper troughing over central Canada/the Upper Midwest and
upper ridging over the western Atlantic, around 20-30 kt of
southwesterly mid-level flow will exist today from the OH Valley
into the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast. Greater destabilization and
steepening of low-level lapse rates are anticipated this afternoon
across the Mid-Atlantic, where recent visible satellite imagery
shows generally clear skies. Loosely organized cells/clusters that
initially develop across the higher terrain of the central
Appalachians should spread into the Mid-Atlantic coastal plain
through the afternoon/evening, while posing a threat for scattered
damaging winds up to 50-60 mph and perhaps marginally severe hail.
Across the OH Valley, somewhat weaker mid-level flow may tend to
limit updraft organization. Still, some potential for clustering and
isolated damaging winds may exist downstream of ongoing convection
where greater destabilization can ocur. Have therefore expanded the
Marginal Risk across much of the OH Valley to account for this
possibility.

...Southern/Central Plains into the Ozarks...
Elevated thunderstorms posing an isolated hail threat in southeast
KS late this morning should further diminish into the early
afternoon as a southwesterly low-level jet gradually weakens. To the
south and east of this activity, a hot and unstable airmass will
exist this afternoon across OK into parts of southern MO and AR.
Although details regarding convective evolution remain unclear, it
is possible that robust thunderstorms develop/continue on the
outflow from this morning's activity, or near multiple MCVs present
from earlier convection. Isolated strong to severe winds appear
possible, even though deep-layer shear should remain weak. The
Marginal Risk has been expanded eastward and connected to the risk
area in the OH Valley. Other isolated thunderstorms posing some
severe wind threat may develop this afternoon farther west across
eastern NM into the OK/TX Panhandles.

...Arizona...
Modest east-southeasterly mid-level flow will persist today over AZ
to the south of a mid/upper-level anticyclone centered over the Four
Corners. Widely scattered convection should develop over the
Mogollon Rim and the higher terrain in southeast AZ this afternoon,
and gradually spread into the lower deserts this evening. Given the
very well-mixed boundary layer and weak to locally moderate
instability expected to be in place ahead of these thunderstorms,
have maintained low severe wind probabilities.

...Northern Nebraska/Southern South Dakota...
Elevated thunderstorms may develop across parts of northern NE and
southern SD late tonight/early Saturday morning as isentropic ascent
increases in tandem with modest strengthening of a southerly
low-level jet. Low-level moistening beneath steepening mid-level
lapse rates should support sufficient MUCAPE for robust updrafts, 
although confidence in overall coverage remains low due to
weak/nebulous large-scale ascent. Regardless, strong shear in the
cloud-bearing layer across this area should promote organized
convection capable of producing isolated severe hail.

..Gleason/Weinman.. 08/07/2026
